title: Under Heaven
author: Kay, Guy Gavriel
review:
The prose is probably the best GGK has written so far, some gorgeous passages. The plot in general GGK style is about some of the littler people in larger conflicts who overlap with those in authority positions, I never usually read GGK for the plot and this one is serviceable but not one of his best; the Sarantine Mosaic probably has my favorite plot that he's written.

The characters are pretty good as well and primarily revolves around a single family and the siblings that are spread across the country.

The themes are great and what I come back to GGK for. Some great meditations on mysticism, spirituality, politics, war and power that are integrated well into the narrative.

GGK really cannot be beat in terms of writing beautiful sections that I want to highlight beginning to end.

highlights.text: But if you couldn’t do everything, did that mean you did nothing?

There was some sadness in how that could happen, Tai thought: falling out of love with something that had shaped you. Or even people who had? But if you didn’t change at least a little, where were the passages of a life? Didn’t learning, changing, sometimes mean letting go of what had once been seen as true?
You have to be afraid for it to count as bravery. Her father had taught her that, a long time ago.
Night clouds, thin moon, stars, But a promise of the sun Remaking the world, Bringing mountains back.
Full moon is falling through the sky. Cranes fly through clouds. Wolves howl. I cannot find rest Because I am powerless To amend a broken world.
The idea we can know what must be done, and do it properly. We cannot know the future, my friend. It claims so much to imagine we can. And the world is not broken any more than it always, always is.”
How we remember changes how we have lived. Time runs both ways. We make stories of our lives.
Sometimes the one life we are allowed is enough.
Tales have many strands, smaller, larger. An incidental figure in one story is living through the drama and passion of his or her own life and death.

And with armies needing to be fed—or they might rebel, themselves—what food could make its way to women and children left at home? If there was a home left. Or children alive. In those years, children were sold for food, or sold as food. Hearts hardened, hearts broke.
